newsitem.title: SPAIN: Chirac, Kohl challenge NATO enlargement costs.
newsitem.headline: Chirac, Kohl challenge NATO enlargement costs.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac said on Wednesday that NATO's eastward enlargement should be achieved at "zero cost" and France would not pay an extra franc towards the alliance's budget to finance it.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl also described cost estimates issued in the United States as manifestly exaggerated in the interests of the military-industrial complex, but U.S. President Bill Clinton said the allies would have to bear "modest costs".
"It is completely absurd to link NATO enlargement with cost factors as if the aim was to rearm large areas of Europe to the teeth," Kohl told a news conference after a two-day NATO summit.
Chirac also said he was sure NATO would invite Romania and Slovenia, excluded from the first wave of alliance enlargement, to join in 1999 when it marks its 50th anniversary.
At his final news conference, the French leader said he was surprised there had been no real discussion of the cost implications among alliance leaders.

"We took a very simple position, that enlargement should be done at zero cost," he said, arguing that there was no longer a military threat in Europe and the alliance needed lighter structures and smaller forces.
"France does not intend to raise its contribution to NATO because of the cost of enlargement," Chirac declared.
Clinton told a news conference that the United States, Canada and the European allies would have to bear "modest costs" for building military infrastructure in the new member states.
Clinton agreed that not enough work had been done on the costs and said many published estimates had been exaggerated and the new member states would pay most of their own costs.
The Clinton administration calculated in February that the cost of expanding NATO into eastern Europe could be $27-35 billion by 2009, without saying how many new members those figures covered.
Chirac cited a NATO document which he said estimated the direct cost to the alliance budget at $1.3 billion for three new members and $1.6 billion for five over the next decade.
The U.S. Congressional budget office has estimated a cost of up to $100-200 billion, while the Rand Corporation, a private American think-tank, put it at $42 billion.

Both Chirac and Kohl said armaments lobbies had a vested interest in suggesting higher costs to sell their wares to new members, but Europe was no longer in a Cold War and NATO's tasks now were essentially peacekeeping and crisis management.

"You can't base your calculations on the assumption these countries will create the same kind of military infrastructure overnight that for instance Germany has," Kohl said, noting that that had taken decades to build during the Cold War.

French officials said it was easy for Chirac to say France would pay no more, since it contributed just five percent of the alliance's infrastructure fund and did not pay towards the integrated military command, which it quit in 1966.

Chirac said he discussed the case of Romania and Slovenia again on Wednesday with Clinton, who on Tuesday had forced through acceptance of only Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic in the first wave.

"The fact is that 1999 is the 50th anniversary of NATO. It's going to be a great celebration for NATO members. I can't imagine that at the next summit on the occasion of this great anniversary, anyone will contest enlargement to Slovenia and Romania which were mentioned by name as deserving," he said.
He also said he believed the first three or four new members would join the European Union in 2000 or 2001.

Chirac said there was no linkage between NATO and EU enlargement and the Europeans would not feel under any pressure to compensate unsuccessful NATO applicants by letting them into the Union if they were not economically qualified.
